name: Student Work and Privacy
title: Student Work and Privacy
answer: Student work such as essays, projects, and test answers counts as part of a student's education record, so pasting it into a general chat tool shares that record with a company the district has no agreement with. Teachers should only use tools covered by a signed data privacy agreement and check the district's approved list before uploading any student work. Removing names is not always enough, because personal writing can identify a student on its own.

sections.body: This idea concerns how teachers handle student work when they use AI tools for feedback and grading. Because essays, projects, and test answers fall under students' education records, sharing them with a tool the district has no agreement with creates a real privacy cost even when the feedback is helpful. The problem it solves is the quiet exposure of student information that can happen when a teacher reaches for a convenient general chat tool. The safe path is to use tools covered by a signed data privacy agreement, which is why many districts provide approved options. Teachers are asked to check the approved list first and to keep student work out of anything not on it.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In day to day classroom use, a teacher checks the district's approved list before putting any student work into a tool. If the tool is not on that list, the work does not go in, no matter how useful the feedback might be. Teachers also think about what a piece of work reveals, since an essay about family, neighborhood, or a personal experience can identify a student even with the name removed. When there is doubt, the teacher either uses an approved tool or gives the feedback personally. The text does not give grade band examples, so the practice applies the same way across year groups.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or finding for this idea, and it does not carry an evidence label. It rests on practice and on the privacy rules described earlier in the book rather than on research. The reasoning offered is that student work forms part of education records and that sharing it with an unapproved company carries a real privacy cost. Readers should treat the guidance as practical advice drawn from district practice, not as a research finding.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits here are clear: student work should not go into any tool that is not on the district's approved list, and a signed data privacy agreement is what makes a tool safe to use. Removing names is not treated as sufficient protection, because personal details in the writing can still identify a student. The decision about whether a tool is appropriate, and the fallback of giving feedback yourself, stays with the teacher. Transparency is also part of the guardrail, since students and families should be told which tools are used for feedback and how the district protects student information. Nothing here is legal advice, and the text describes practice rather than setting out rules.
